t: How Best To Hold Students Accountable
q: Why does it pain teachers to hold students accountable? Why are some so quick to ignore misbehavior, look the other way, or make excuses for it?
The it’s-not-me-it’s-you strategy is a personal reminder that student misbehavior is not about you. It’s about them.
You are bound by your classroom management plan and therefore have but one choice when a student misbehaves: enforce a consequence.
Rest assured, holding your students accountable is an act of compassion.
Your students will adopt the same attitude. They will mentally separate the consequence (which they’ve earned of their own accord) from the enforcer (which is you).

There are scores of teachers willing to lighten the load on their students by ignoring poor behavior, looking the other way, or giving second chances. And by doing so, they are harming their chances for success.
x: Holding students accountable consistently is ultimately an act of compassion, not harshness.
The 'it's-not-me-it's-you' strategy reframes misbehavior as entirely the student's choice and responsibility, not the teacher's burden.

The idea is that misbehavior is entirely a student's choice and responsibility; the teacher's only role is to enforce the classroom management plan, which removes personal guilt or hesitation from the equation.

t: Why You Need Leverage For Classroom Management… And How To Get It
q: The key to effective classroom management is leverage. If your students like being part of your classroom, then you have leverage, and accountability will work the way it’s supposed to.
Done correctly, a teacher’s leverage can become so powerful and so influential that even the toughest students need no more than a glance to curb behavior. That is no exaggeration.
Regardless of where you teach or who your students are, the power of leverage can transform your students into the class you really want.

Teachers seeking to improve classroom management tend to focus on finding the right combination of rules, consequences, and rewards that will work for them. These are important, no doubt. But what makes them go, what makes them effective, is leverage.
The idea is to create a tsunami of leverage so wide and deep that no student can resist its power.
You’ll discover your influence with students growing right along with your love of teaching and everything—classroom management, motivation, attentiveness, academic performance—becoming much easier.
x: Leverage—students' genuine desire to be part of the classroom—is the foundational force that makes consequences and classroom management work.
Building enough leverage can make even the toughest students responsive to nothing more than a glance from the teacher.

Rules, consequences, and rewards are secondary; leverage is what makes those tools actually effective.

t: How To Teach Without Getting Stressed-Out; Arghhh!
q: I have a technique you can start using tomorrow that will eliminate stress from your teaching life. This no-stress method is so effective, in fact, that many professional athletes use it before a competition.

When I made the decision to become a teacher, I decided that I was going to love my job no matter the circumstances. I wasn’t going to sit back and see if I was going to be fulfilled, happy, or having fun.
The students began to feed off of my calm energy. And every day I gained greater control and respect.
He said that, before a match, if they will make a conscience decision to keep their composure—despite the adversity they may face—then remarkably, they will.
Being stress free in the classroom, as well as on the tennis court, is a decision you make. Stress doesn’t happen to you; you let it happen to you.
Your calm, confident demeanor will sweep the negative and excitable energy out of your classroom.
x: Linsin shares his 'decide-first method' of stress relief, a technique he stumbled into as an overwhelmed student teacher and later found echoed in sports psychology advice about athletes managing competitive nerves.
The 'decide-first method' involves consciously deciding, before the school day begins, to stay emotionally unaffected no matter what happens.
A teacher's calm internal state visibly spreads to students, who respond to and mirror what they sense from the teacher.
Sports psychology supports the same principle: athletes who decide beforehand to keep composure despite adversity are more likely to do so.

q: Clip charts, prize boxes, incentive systems, seating arrangements, stickers, pep-talks, noise makers, red cards, table points, trinkets, tokens, awards, erasers, free time, computer time, first in line, contracts, privileges, and… enough!!!
For many, classroom management has become too complicated. It doesn’t need to be. All you need are a few guiding principles.
You have to be willing to enforce a consequence every time a rule is broken. This is critical to effective classroom management. Most teachers don’t follow through consistently.
Creating a fun, stimulating learning environment covers up a multitude of classroom management mistakes. Kids who like school behave better—a lot better.
If your students like/love being in your classroom, they won’t want to be separated from it. This is what makes time-out work.
Your students must know what to expect every time they enter your classroom. Therefore, you must be consistently pleasant.
x: Reacting against the clutter of clip charts, prize boxes, and incentive systems that dominate many classrooms, Linsin argues classroom management can be stripped down to a handful of core principles.
Classroom management can be reduced to a handful of guiding principles rather than a clutter of charts, prizes, and incentive systems.
Core principles include comprehensive rules, consistent consequence enforcement, and genuine willingness to follow through every time.
